en.title: Sort Product Codes by a Custom Unicode Character Order
en.description:
order lists the characters from smallest to largest. To compare two product codes, look at the first character where they differ; if one is a prefix of the other, the shorter one is smaller. Keep duplicate codes and return the sorted result. Characters are counted as Unicode code points, not as UTF-16 surrogate units.

This site independently wrote the standard I/O, editorial and tests; missing original bounds and corrections to examples are stated explicitly in the statement.
en.input: The input is a JSON array [order,productCodes], which may contain standard JSON whitespace and escapes. The original constraints are truncated and give no complete count or character domain; on this site order contains 1..256 distinct Unicode scalar values, 1≤number of codes≤100000, and the total length of all codes is ≤1000000 code points. Codes may be empty, and every character appears in order; spaces, control characters, NUL and non-BMP characters are kept, and lone surrogates are not allowed. The total UTF-8 input budget is 16MiB (the standard compact worst case is under 12303100 bytes).
en.output: Output a canonical compact ASCII JSON array of strings, with only commas between elements and no extra structural whitespace. Quotes and backslashes are written as \" and \\; backspace/tab/newline/form feed/carriage return are written as \b/\t/\n/\f/\r; the remaining U+0000..001F and every code point from U+007F upward use lowercase hexadecimal \uXXXX, with non-BMP characters split into UTF-16 surrogate pairs; U+0020..007E other than quotes and backslashes are output directly, including the space and /. End with a single newline. This output convention only normalizes the encoding and removes no characters.
en.explanation: The outputs of the three public examples are ["abc","adc"]; ["","b","b","ba","a"]; and ["","\ud83d\ude00","\ud83d\ude00a","\u0000"," ","a"], checked by independent enumeration or direct simulation.
hints: Build a mapping from characters to their order 0..255, turn each string into a byte sort key of the same length, and sort the original strings by the lexicographic order of these byte strings.
